title: Nursing Management, Education and Research
description: Leadership and management in nursing, ward and unit administration, nursing law and ethics in Nigeria, clinical teaching and education, and research and evidence-based practice.

topics.title: Leadership and Management in Nursing
topics.summary: Management functions, leadership styles, motivation, delegation and conflict management.

notes.b: Management functions (Fayol; Gulick's POSDCORB): planning, organising, staffing, directing (leading, coordinating), and controlling (evaluating, budgeting, reporting). Leadership styles: autocratic (quick decisions, useful in emergencies, may lower morale), democratic/participative (involves staff, increases commitment), laissez-faire (minimal direction — suits highly skilled teams, risky otherwise), transformational (inspires a shared vision and change), transactional (rewards and corrective action) and situational (adapts to staff readiness — Hersey and Blanchard). Nurse managers in Nigeria (chief nursing officers, matrons, ward managers) face staff shortages, high workload, emigration of nurses ('japa'), limited resources and industrial actions. Motivation theories: Maslow's hierarchy of needs, Herzberg's two-factor theory (hygiene factors — salary, conditions; motivators — recognition, achievement, responsibility), and McGregor's Theory X and Y. Change management: Lewin's model — unfreeze, change (move), refreeze.

Delegation transfers authority to perform a task while the delegating nurse retains accountability; the five rights of delegation: right task, right circumstance, right person, right direction/communication and right supervision/evaluation. Tasks requiring nursing judgement (assessment, care planning, evaluation, health education of unstable patients) should not be delegated to unqualified staff. Conflict in teams arises from role ambiguity, scarce resources, communication problems and personality differences; resolution strategies (Thomas–Kilmann): avoiding, accommodating, competing, compromising and collaborating (win–win — usually best). Effective communication (SBAR handovers), time management, decision-making and teamwork underpin safe care. Staffing: patient classification systems estimate workload; rostering must balance skill mix, fairness and rest. Performance appraisal provides feedback and identifies training needs.

topics.title: Ward Administration and Quality of Care
topics.summary: Records and reports, resource management, quality improvement and patient safety.

notes.b: Ward management includes planning and organising care (nursing care models — functional/task nursing, team nursing, primary nursing, patient allocation), staff rostering, admission, transfer and discharge processes, handover, ward rounds, management of supplies and equipment (inventory, stock control, maintenance, prevention of theft and waste), infection prevention, and maintaining a safe environment. Nursing records (admission records, nursing process documentation, observation charts, fluid balance, drug administration records, incident reports, ward reports) must be accurate, contemporaneous, legible, signed and dated — they are legal documents ('not documented, not done'). Confidentiality of records is required. Electronic health records are gradually being adopted in Nigerian hospitals.
k: Care models: task, team, primary, allocation

notes.b: Quality of care has dimensions of safety, effectiveness, patient-centredness, timeliness, efficiency and equity (Institute of Medicine). Donabedian's model evaluates structure (resources, staff, equipment), process (activities of care) and outcome (results — mortality, infection rates, satisfaction). Quality improvement tools: clinical audit (set standards, measure practice, compare, implement change, re-audit — the audit cycle), PDSA cycles, root cause analysis of adverse events, and fishbone diagrams. Patient safety culture encourages incident reporting without blame (just culture), learning from near misses, and implementing safety practices: correct patient identification (two identifiers), safe medication administration (rights of medication administration), falls prevention, pressure ulcer prevention, hand hygiene and safe surgery checklists. Accreditation programmes (e.g. SafeCare standards) assess facility quality in Nigeria.

topics.title: Nursing Law, Ethics and Professional Regulation in Nigeria
topics.summary: NMCN, scope of practice, ethical principles, legal issues and professional misconduct.

notes.b: The Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN), established under the Nursing and Midwifery (Registration, etc.) Act (Cap N143 LFN 2004), regulates nursing and midwifery education and practice: accrediting schools, conducting licensing examinations, registering and licensing nurses and midwives (licence renewal every three years with mandatory continuing professional development), setting standards and a Code of Professional Conduct, and disciplining practitioners through the Nursing and Midwifery Tribunal. Professional bodies include the National Association of Nigerian Nurses and Midwives (NANNM). Nursing education has progressed from hospital-based schools to university degrees (BNSc) and postgraduate programmes. Nurses must work within their scope of practice; task-shifting policies (e.g. community health officers) define expanded roles in specific settings.

Ethical principles: autonomy (informed consent, respecting refusal by competent adults), beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, veracity (truthfulness), fidelity (keeping promises), and confidentiality. Legal concepts: negligence (duty of care, breach, causation, damage), malpractice, assault and battery (touching without consent), false imprisonment (unlawful restraint), defamation (libel — written; slander — spoken), and vicarious liability (employers liable for employees' acts in the course of employment). Consent: informed, voluntary, by a competent person; parents or guardians consent for minors; emergencies permit treatment without consent under necessity. Documentation protects nurses legally. Ethical dilemmas common in Nigeria: requests to conceal diagnoses (e.g. HIV, cancer) from patients, resource allocation, detaining patients for unpaid bills (unlawful), religious objections to treatment, and care at the end of life. Professional misconduct includes abandonment of patients, falsification of records, drug theft, sexual misconduct and practising without a licence.
k: Detaining patients for bills is unlawful

topics.title: Nursing Education and Clinical Teaching
topics.summary: Learning theories, curriculum, clinical teaching methods, assessment and preceptorship.

notes.b: Learning theories: behaviourism (learning through reinforcement — skills drills, feedback), cognitivism (mental processing and understanding — concept maps), constructivism (learners build knowledge from experience — problem-based learning), social learning (Bandura — observation and role modelling; clinical role models matter), humanism (learner-centred, self-directed — Rogers, Maslow), and adult learning (andragogy — Knowles: adults are self-directed, draw on experience, and want relevant, problem-centred learning). Learning domains (Bloom's taxonomy): cognitive (knowledge to evaluation/creation), affective (attitudes and values) and psychomotor (skills). Learning objectives should be specific and measurable (SMART) using action verbs. Teaching methods: lectures, discussions, demonstrations and return demonstrations, simulation (skills labs, manikins), case studies, problem-based learning, and e-learning (increasingly used in Nigeria since COVID-19).

Clinical learning is central to nursing education; effective clinical teaching includes orientation, clear objectives, supervised practice, demonstration and return demonstration, reflective practice (Gibbs' reflective cycle — description, feelings, evaluation, analysis, conclusion, action plan), case presentations, nursing rounds and feedback (timely, specific and constructive). Preceptorship pairs a new nurse or student with an experienced nurse; mentorship supports longer-term professional development. Assessment: formative (during learning, for feedback) and summative (at the end, for grading/certification); methods include written tests, OSCE (Objective Structured Clinical Examination), practical examinations, logbooks and portfolios, and continuous clinical assessment. Validity (measures what it should) and reliability (consistency) are key qualities of assessment. Patient education applies the same principles: assess learning needs and readiness, plan, implement and evaluate (e.g. teach-back).

topics.title: Nursing Research and Evidence-Based Practice
topics.summary: Research process, designs, sampling, data collection, ethics, and applying evidence.

notes.b: The research process: identify a problem, review literature, state objectives/hypotheses, choose a design, define population and sample, develop instruments, obtain ethical approval, collect data, analyse, interpret and disseminate. Quantitative designs: descriptive (cross-sectional surveys — common in Nigerian nursing research), correlational, quasi-experimental and experimental (RCTs). Qualitative designs: phenomenology (lived experience), grounded theory (generating theory), ethnography (culture) and case studies; data from in-depth interviews and focus group discussions analysed thematically. Mixed methods combine both. Sampling: probability (simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster — generalisable) and non-probability (convenience, purposive, snowball, quota). Instruments must be valid and reliable (pilot testing; Cronbach's alpha for internal consistency ≥ 0.7). Statistics: descriptive (frequencies, means, SD) and inferential (chi-square, t-test, ANOVA, correlation; p < 0.05).

Research ethics: respect for persons (informed consent, voluntary participation, right to withdraw), beneficence and non-maleficence (minimise risk), justice (fair selection), confidentiality and anonymity; approval from a health research ethics committee (NHREC-registered in Nigeria; the National Code of Health Research Ethics); special protection for vulnerable groups. Evidence-based practice (EBP) integrates the best research evidence, clinical expertise and patient values and preferences. Steps: ask a focused clinical question (PICO — Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome), acquire evidence (databases — PubMed, CINAHL, Cochrane), appraise it critically, apply it, and assess the outcome. The hierarchy of evidence places systematic reviews and RCTs highest. Barriers to EBP in Nigeria include limited access to journals and internet, workload, lack of skills and organisational culture; strategies include journal clubs, EBP training and nurse-led research.
